subtopic: TUNGSTEN

speechtext:
During the last war the government opened up a deposit of tungsten in a property known as the Emerald mine. A makeshift mill was erected, and tungsten ore was mined until the end of the war. Upon the conclusion of the war the price of tungsten would not permit the mine to carry on as a commercial operation. After tenders had been invited, it was sold to the Canadian Exploration Company for $950,000, which has been paid.
The demand for tungsten is again active, and we have repurchased that portion of the property which contained the known tungsten values, for a price of $328,000, which is exactly the same amount as was included in the sale price to the present owners. In other words, we bought the tungsten property back at the same price as that at which we sold it. We are now building a more suitable mill. The owners of the Emerald property have been mining lead and zinc, as well as conducting other operations on the property, and they will supervise the installation of the new mill on the tungsten property and operate it for government account.

subtopic: VICTORIA AND JACQUES CARTIER, ST. LAWRENCE RIVER  ABOLITION OF TOLLS

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, February 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pinard:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into early consideration the advisability of abolishing the tolls imposed and collected on the Victoria and Jacques Cartier bridges over the St. Lawrence river.

subtopic: VICTORIA AND JACQUES CARTIER, ST. LAWRENCE RIVER  ABOLITION OF TOLLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last evening I was about to make a few remarks on this resolution, which was so ably presented by its sponsor, the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Pinard).
The resolution has already been read. I am not going to go into the details of it. I want to speak only on the principle of the resolution. Its sponsor certainly excelled himself in his speech. He is well known to the house as one of the greatest debaters the province of Quebec has ever produced; and I congratulate him on his presentation of the subject. The others who followed him spoke in the same language as he did, their native tongue. I am not going to try to make any remarks in that language, because I know that if I got started, someone would shout: ne touchez pas! I am going to try to keep to my native language, be my speech good, bad or indifferent.
The principle of this resolution is the abolition of tolls that have been imposed and collected on certain bridges. What is a toll? On looking the word up in the dictionary I find that a toll is a charge payable for permission to pass a barrier. Any bridge or highway connecting two other highways or towns or villages is always known as a king's highway, whether it is owned federally or provincially; and there can be no barrier, even at any price, placed on a king's highway.
The principle that I want to vote for is the abolition of an old, obsolete system, that of tolls on the king's highways. It matters not who built this bridge, but it does matter who at the present time owns it and where the tolls are going. From what has been said by some of those who have spoken, I understand that it is a three-way division: municipal, provincial and federal. However, the principle of the resolution which has been under discussion is the abolition of the toll; they do not want tolls any more. It is certainly obsolete to have them.

The reason I am supporting the resolution is this. One of the hon. members who spoke said that if on these two bridges the tolls were abolished, there would be no other bridges in Quebec exacting tolls from the people; there would be no more toll bridges in that province. The point I want to make -and I wish it had been attached to this resolution-has to do with the toll bridge across the Hillsborough river between Charlottetown and Southport, Prince Edward Island. Prior to the building of that bridge there was a ferry system for the accommodation of the public. The bridge was built to accommodate the railway that was built from Southport to Murray Harbour, and it was supposed to be wide enough to take care of vehicular traffic as well. When building this bridge for the railway, the government said that it would be a toll bridge. The provincial government of that time did not wish it to be a toll bridge. However, the toll had to be paid, and the provincial government, rather than discriminate against people living on the south side of the river, decided, out of the taxpayers' money, to pay the toll and also to keep in repair the planking on both sides of the rails for a length of over a mile. That toll, together with the repairs, amounts to some $10,000 a year. The principle is wrong, just the same as it is with reference to the Victoria and Jacques Cartier bridges.
During the last forty-six years this bridge, which was obsolete when it was put there because it was a secondhand bridge from some place up the Restigouche, has cost $10,000 a year. The bridge was obsolete forty-five or fifty years ago; today it is condemned as unsafe for heavy traffic, and freight traffic has to be routed over another line down through Murray Harbour.
As a province we should not have to continue paying this amount of almost $10,000 annually, as we have done for nearly forty-six years. In other words, we have paid the cost of the bridge twice over, and have nothing in the end but a bridge condemned in the first instance for heavy traffic, and now condemned for automobile traffic and trucks as well.
I urge upon the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), although it does not come within the scope of this resolution, that he consider giving us the right to do away with the payment of this $10,000 a year for a bridge that is now condemned by the railway people themselves.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest yesterday to the complete and eloquent plea made by the hon.
Tolls on Quebec bridges member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Pinard) regarding the toll payable on the Victoria bridge. This bridge is in my riding. I believe toll has been collected on it for the past seventy-five years, and it would be a great benefit to the people of Montreal if this toll were eliminated.
My purpose in rising is to support the resolution of the hon. member. subtopic: VICTORIA AND JACQUES CARTIER, ST. LAWRENCE RIVER  ABOLITION OF TOLLS
speechtext:
I listened with deep interest to the
speeches made yesterday and this afternoon in connection with this resolution which appears on the order paper and reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into early consideration the advisability of abolishing the tolls imposed and collected on the Victoria and Jacques Cartier bridges over the St. Lawrence river.
This resolution was very well discussed by the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Pinard) who has been requesting such action for several sessions, as well as by the other members who have supported it. The hon. member for Chambly-Rouville put this motion on the order paper several times because he believes the settling of this matter is important to his electors and to the great many people living on the south shore who use these bridges to cross the St. Lawrence river.
However I must point out to the house that there are two sides to the question involved in this resolution. There is the legal side and the practical side.
Before going any further on this matter I wish to offer the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville my special congratulations for the manner in which he has introduced his resolution. It makes it unnecessary for me to repeat the arguments he has advanced and which I could very well make mine under the circumstances.
But let us consider the two aspects of this matter. First, we must examine the legal aspect. It should be borne in mind that there is an agreement between three parties: the national harbours board, through its predecessor the Montreal harbour commission, the municipality of the city of Montreal and

Tulls on Quebec bridges the province of Quebec. Certain members seemed to forget, in the discussion this afternoon and yesterday, this agreement whereby three governments, federal, provincial and municipal have undertaken to pay one-third of the cost of maintenance providing it does not exceed the amount of $150,000 a year.
As was so ably stated last night by the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville, the city of Montreal stopped paying its share at least since 1944. It was therefore necessary to take action against the city of Montreal. A decision was brought down in favour of the national harbours board, but the matter is now before the court of appeal.
It is now a matter of deciding whether tolls should be abolished and if from now on costs should be charged to the federal government, the provincial government, or the city of Montreal.
I also wish to congratulate the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) on his speech, in which he said something to the effect that the toll system is detrimental to the people of the province of Quebec and that the dominion government should assume its cost.
I do not think there can be any disagreement in principle as to the elimination of tolls. In principle we favour doing away with the toll system. There is no difficulty on that point. But we have to decide who should bear the costs. As regards jurisdiction, moreover, the three parties have already come to an agreement. To my mind, tolls cannot be removed unless there is some agreement on the procedure to be followed. It goes without saying that, for the time being, this agreement concerns only the Jacques Cartier bridge. Nor should hon. members forget that the agreement which related to the building of the Montreal bridge, the Jacques Cartier bridge, was signed following the enactment of a statute by the house, the passing of legislation by the provincial legislature and the approval of a minute by the city of Montreal.
Therefore, I submit that the suppression of the tolls would necessitate the agreement of the three parties concerned.
We must also consider the practical side of the matter which is no less important than its legal aspect. In 1950, the national harbours board collected, I believe, $1,200,000 in tolls on Jacques Cartier bridge. As for Victoria bridge, I cannot give you any idea of the amount collected since it is buried in the accounts of the Canadian National Railways.


What I mean is this. It is not easy for the national harbours board or for the Canadian National to give up without further ado revenues exceeding a million dollars.
Hon. members are constantly asking that we reduce expenditures. How would they explain the relinquishment of such an important source of income? That is the practical side of the matter. The money would have to be found elsewhere.
If we give up this source of revenue, the house will have to find means of collecting the money needed to wipe out the deficit that would inevitably follow. In other words, we would have to impose an additional burden on every citizen.
As regards Victoria bridge, I have already informed the house that, on the condition mentioned in Hansard, the Canadian National Railways were ready to consider the removal of tolls now levied. The Canadian National has already indicated its approval of legislation that would do away with tolls for noncommercial passengers. The removal of tolls is based on the contingency of a satisfactory agreement with the province. This agreement would compensate the Canadian National for monetary losses sustained and would also protect its interests.
I do not believe the house would wish to proceed on any other basis because, after all, if we gave up revenue adding up to $1 million or $2 million, we would have to find it elsewhere.
(Text):
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I might sum up briefly and rapidly what I have said, so that the house may know the nature of the resolution which seeks the abolition of tolls on two bridges crossing the St. Lawrence river at Montreal, namely the Victoria and the Harbour bridge.
The reasons I have submitted, one the legal and the other practical, indicate that it is impossible to consider the abolition of these tolls at this time unless there is some agreement with the parties concerned, namely the province of Quebec, the city of Montreal, and the national harbours board.
I have already stated in the house on one occasion, if not on two, that the federal government, through its agency, the national harbours board, is prepared to receive representations and, if need be, to enter into negotiations for the abolition of these tolls. But

it must be understood that the abolition could not be made at the exclusive expense of the federal government.
The hon. member for Chambly-Rouville, who has so well presented his motion, ably supported by other members from the south shore and elsewhere, may feel that the object they had in mind, namely, a full discussion of the important question of the abolition of tolls on these bridges, has served its purpose. If the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville feels that the motion has served that purpose, perhaps he would give consideration at this time to withdrawing it.

subtopic: EQUALIZING OF OPPORTUNITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this resolution is to bring to the attention of the government the desirability of equalizing educational opportunity across Canada.

Education
This matter has been debated for several sessions, and I have spoken at some length on every similar proposal that has been before the house. I might say that I was disappointed on May 22 last to hear the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) speak at some length in opposition to a similar resolution. It was disappointing to hear members of the government express themselves as they did at that time.
I do not need to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the cost of education has been a vital issue for many years in the province of Manitoba from which I come. The municipal corporations have had to provide for the cost of education by a levy on real estate that averages $3 for every $1 provided by the government of Manitoba. Everyone must realize chat you cannot have equality of educational opportunity under such a system. It is just impossible.
This has been a vital issue at the last three annual gatherings of the municipal convention of Manitoba, and also at the annual convention of the trustees of Manitoba. It has been a vital issue for some years. By contrast I should like to indicate what has been done in Ontario. I would remind the house that the leader of this party, when he was premier of Ontario and minister of education, provided for very progressive legislation for education in the province of Ontario. In some school districts the province finances as much as ninety per cent of the cost. We have an important comparison right there. I should like to quote one paragraph from a speech made by my leader in this house on a similar resolution, to be found at page 944 of Hansard of October 19, 1949. He said:
There is, however, this important consideration which cannot be emphasized too often. Even if we built in Canada the finest schools that have ever been constructed anywhere, we would have done nothing to advance our educational standards unless those who are teaching in those schools are highly qualified to teach the children that come under their direction. For that reason, wherever the school may be and whatever type of school may be under consideration, the effort of all those concerned with the advancement of education in Canada should be to raise to a level that is in keeping with their responsibility the salaries of those to whom we are entrusting to a considerable extent the whole future of Canada.
There is a lot of meaning in that statement which was placed on the record by the leader of this party when a similar resolution was before this house on a previous occasion.
I do not want to take time to repeat the arguments that have been made in this debate and that I have placed on the record

in the course of debates in the past on similar resolutions. But I want to emphasize the fact that real estate cannot properly provide for the cost of education, and certainly cannot provide for equality of educational opportunity in this country. It is just an utter impossibility, and it should not be expected to do so.
I support wholeheartedly this resolution. I hope that we are to be permitted to vote on it this afternoon, and that the house will endorse it. It is one of the most important matters that can engage the attention of Canadians in these times. It is important because it aims at the providing of equality of educational opportunity for the young people of this land. They are the people who will be responsible for this country in the years to come, and I know of nothing more important.

subtopic: EQUALIZING OF OPPORTUNITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few remarks I should like to make on this resolution. Perhaps I have an obligation in a personal way, as I happen to be on the board of trustees of a university which hopes to be one of the beneficiaries of the plan which we hope is under consideration. In passing, I should like to associate myself with what has been said previously about provincial responsibility in connection with education. To put it mildly, we have been encouraged to hope that the time will soon come when consideration will be given to us and to other universities.
I might say just one word about our university, to indicate the problem which affects us and which in varying degree affects other people as well. More than a century ago Queen's university at Kingston was founded by the Presbyterian church. I am quick to say that there never has been any religious test, except that for the first few decades the university constitution required that the principal should be a minister of the Presbyterian church. As time went on it became difficult to carry on the affairs of the university, although we were receiving generous assistance from people of all creeds. Some forty years ago the difficulties of financing became so great that the Presbyterian church, with great generosity, handed the university over to the public. Since then there have been no religion tests of any kind, not even of the principal.
We have tried to paddle our own canoe as best we could. We believe we have a loyal body of graduates. Sometimes I fear we become a little tiresome to other people by talking about the loyalty of our graduates. But it is a real thing, and they have helped us, not merely with words but with deeds. We have received generous subscriptions; in fact

Education
at the present time we are trying to get the beneficence of the graduates on an annual basis by having them make annual gifts.
Notwithstanding all that, great difficulties still exist. Not only do they exist, they are increasing. Taxation of all kinds makes it more difficult as the years go by to get outside assistance. Since we separated ourselves, almost forty years ago, from any technical connection with the Presbyterian church, we have received generous aid from the province of Ontario. As I have indicated, we have done our best to increase our own resources, and of course fees also play a large part. But the difficulty is still great.
I should like to take a few minutes to indicate a special form that that difficulty has taken. I do this because it is something that alarms me. I think I can best indicate what I have in mind by referring briefly to a remark made not long ago by the president of the university of Toronto, Dr. Sidney Smith, in connection with the ever-recurring question of university salaries. I think we all ought to feel responsible for the fact that our teaching profession is not treated better than it is. I think one of the best tests of the level of the civilization of any community is the way they treat the teaching profession. If the teaching profession is well treated, that is evidence of a high state of civilization. Dr. Smith recently made a statement in connection with salaries, and said that he was afraid they were going to be driven to paying less to those professors who deal with what might be called the non-vocational subjects, that is, subjects which you do not cash in on the day you leave the university. These are the subjects, of course, which once were regarded as the extreme and almost the exclusive object of education.
I am sure Dr. Smith made that suggestion only with the greatest regret. Dr. Cyril James of McGill university said that a double standard, as he called it, would be a matter of grave loss to Canadian universities; and from communicating with him I know that our own principal at Queen's university, Dr. Wallace, who is well known in university circles, has exactly the same feeling.
I want to develop this a little because the very fact that this could happen suggests to me that our attitude toward education might well be very carefully considered. Let me remind you too, Mr. Speaker, that professors other than those teaching what we usually call the humanities find it much easier to supplement their university salaries. Doctors teaching in universities for the most part have their professional incomes as well. Engineers and other vocational teachers have
a much greater opportunity to add substantially to their incomes by doing various kinds of expert work during the vacation. Not only are they to have that advantage, but Dr. Smith is even constrained to suggest that in addition they might perhaps have higher salaries than other professors.
The best teachers, of course, do not teach because of the money. I remember an old professor of mine who was getting me to help him with his income tax one day. He was then getting the munificent salary of $6,000 a year; that was in Toronto. He said, "Think of that, Jim. We never got that at Kingston in those days. Think of me getting $6,000 a year. Why, in the old days at Queen's I would have been glad to have $2,000 and to be sure that would not shrink." I said, "I don't agree with that at all. You should have the salary of a bank president." He replied, "But look at the kind of work I am doing. Why, if I were a man of means I would pay a premium to be allowed to do it." That spirit is not universal, of course; nevertheless it is present, or we would not have the men we have carrying on this work.
I want to take just a few minutes of the time of the house to say a word about this subject, and to quote a remark made by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray) the other day, part of which I applaud most heartily and with part of which I want to disagree. After referring to various minerals which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) had said we needed, the hon. member went on to add, at page 473 of Hansard:
Our war effort will fail if we do not secure supplies of these vital strategic war metals from some place in the world.
Of course that is true. Then he went on:
I think we might very well encourage the mining schools at Queen's university-
And of course that is true.
-the university of British Columbia and elsewhere across this country, so that research might be carried on-
And that is true, too; I would not disagree with a word of it. Then this is the part I want to question, if I understand the hon. member correctly. He went on to say:
So my suggestion is that we leave these academic discussions and speeches, which were popular in the earlier days when we were not faced with the severe trials now ahead of us, and become more objective.
I am very glad the hon. member was so frank, because I believe that view is widely held. If I understand the hon. gentleman correctly he is really saying, by implication, that life is real and earnest now; that we have to deal with these material things, and have to set the other things aside. If that

Education
were to happen for three months or six months, though it is extremely difficult to see how it could be done, one might feel that perhaps it had to be considered; but in the situation in which we find ourselves, when we do not know how long it is going to last, I would suggest two things to the hon. member. First of all I would suggest that, perhaps to an extent we can hardly realize and certainly we can never prove, the present plight in which we find ourselves is due to the fact that for some time we have disregarded these things. I say to him further that if this testing time through which we are passing now should last five years or ten years, as it may, then it seems to me there never was a time when we were in so much need of these things which the hon. member says in effect cannot now occupy the attention of serious men in an emergency. I do not wish to press his words unduly because I think I understand the way in which he meant them.
Pursuing that subject just a little further I should like to quote some words, grave words, you may think exaggerated words, which nevertheless come from a high source, Mr. Walter Lippmann, a man whose opinions we value. These comments were made some years ago with respect to education in the United States. I stress the fact that it was education in the United States. I am sure also that what I am about to read will not apply to certain universities that have tried to keep the flag of real education flying, but I ask hon. members to listen to these comments, which are quite brief, and ask themselves whether in fact Mr. Lippmann does not utter a grave warning.
I want to digress for a moment, because I wish to read the words used by Dr. Sidney Smith of the university of Toronto before I quote Mr. Lippmann. This is Dr. Smith's last report, which appeared just a few weeks ago. He deals with this matter, and I want to refer briefly to what he has to say so that when I read the quotation from Mr. Lippmann hon. members will have in mind the words used by Dr. Smith:
Any claim that the university is offering a liberal education to all its students must be based in considerable measure on the emphasis given to the humanities. It is relatively easy to obtain financial support for the physical and biological sciences. Public interest in the social sciences, for example, economics, is high and it is increasing. Canadians pay lip service to the humanities but frequently their tribute ends there.
Now, reiterating my warning that these comments by Mr. Lippmann are directed to education in the United States and also that I think many universities, particularly those which have maintained close association with

churches, do not come under this condemnation to anything like the extent others do, I read these short passages. Mr. Lippmann says:
The thesis which I venture to submit to you is as follows:
That during the past forty or fifty years those who are responsible for education have progressively removed from the curriculum of studies the western culture which produced the modern democratic state.
I think you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that that is a plain statement of fact; that the institutions by which we live were produced by this western culture which Lippmann argues we are now disregarding. Then he goes on:
That, deprived of their cultural tradition, the newly educated western men no longer possess in the form and substance of their own minds and spirits, the ideas, the premises, the rationale, the logic, the method, the values or the deposited wisdom which are the genius of the development of western civilization.
Then he adds:
That the prevailing education is destined, if it continues, to destroy western civilization and is in fact destroying it.
Again I remind hon. members that those words were not addressed to us, but I suggest we might well consider them. There is only one other short quotation I should like to read:
Modem education, however, is based on a denial that it is necessary or useful or desirable for the schools and colleges to continue to transmit from generation, to generation the religious and classical culture of the western world.
As I say, those are grave words, and I have read them to the house because I believe we live in grave times. We talk quite often about our way of life, and equally often in vehement phrases of detestation of this strange new madness, as it seems to us, that has arisen and to which we are opposed. We speak of it as fanaticism, but if you look up the dictionary meaning of "fanaticism", you will And that there is a kind of belief, even though it is a mistaken belief, included in it. This recalls to mind some very searching words used by a well known journalist in western Canada, Bruce Hutchison. Speaking about this very problem some eighteen months ago he uttered words which I have never been able to get out of my mind. I hear people talking about our way of life, and I have often wondered whether it means motor cars, hockey matches, and all that kind of thing. What else does it mean? Incidentally, Mr. Hutchison pointed out that in this strange and horrible fanaticism, as we regard it, there is a certain element of faith-I believe he used the word "faith" and if not I adopt it as my own. Then he

Education
said that we may be in danger of finding that we are opposing the communist something with a nothing.
I should like to add one thing, Mr. Speaker. It seems to me that those of us who are older have inherited a kind of spiritual legacy from our fathers, a legacy of the rule of law, and all the other things which have gone into making up life. We have now drifted into a situation where these things are no longer as clear as they used to be. I have often thought of a wise remark made by a former governor general, Lord Tweedsmuir, to the effect that our difficulty is not to choose between right and wrong, but to choose between two rights. It seems to me we are now confused by the number of problems that are facing us. As the member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray) said, we have to have regard for all those material things which are necessary for our salvation'. I suggest also that in the end it is morale that is going to count, and in the end morale depends on morals. It depends on having something we really and truly do believe. I go back therefore, Mr. Speaker, to this question of education, and I do urge that we remind ourselves, as Lippmann says, that true education does not exist without a real knowledge or understanding of this civilization in which we live, and which is based on western culture.

Mr. Speaker, it has been said by members from the opposite side of the house that they do not wish to have this resolution talked out. During this session, however, according to my calculations there have been twenty-two speakers on this question, and about eighteen of them have been from the opposition. I do not propose to take very much of the time of the house, therefore, because I may be accused of attempting to talk out the resolution. Certainly, there is plenty of time ahead of us, so we can be sure it will not be talked out.
I did not come prepared to speak on this question this afternoon. I thought a labour bill would be coming up, and I was prepared to discuss it. I regret that it has been subordinated to this other important question of giving the provinces assistance in the matter of education. Everyone who has spoken from the Conservative party benches, and the C.C.F., has spoken in favour of this resolution. Being in favour of it, they have not advanced any of the reasons why the members who support the government should have any objections to such a resolution. I am opposing this resolution at this time. In opposing the resolution I do not wish to indicate in any way that I feel education is not of primary importance. I believe, in fact,
that it has been the No. 1 factor in our survival as a great nation. Throughout the discussion no one has attempted to separate their arguments on the value of education from the manner in which it should be administered.
I cannot see how it will be possible to reduce the cost of education and, at the same time, increase the opportunity for education merely by putting the responsibility upon the federal government. The B.N.A. Act provides that education is a provincial responsibility. Everyone is familiar with the principle that a line has no end, and can be extended to any length. If education is the primary responsibility of the provinces, then by extending this line we would be creating a precedent, and we have no reason for assuming that other provincial responsibilities may not, at some future date, be brought to the door of the federal authority. It is my humble opinion that the federal government should raise sufficient funds through taxation to carry out its responsibilities as a federal authority, and not to interfere in such matters.
Who are the people who are requesting this federal aid? We have resolutions from school boards, and we have resolutions from the teachers' associations. In many instances school boards have found that in building new schools they have to expend more money than the fields of taxation now open to them will allow. I know that the teachers' federations fully appreciate the difficulties of the school boards. They are the employee group, however, and I have a feeling that their primary concern in the matter of federal aid is the hope that it will increase the rate of pay to their profession. If the federal authority is to make grants directly for educational purposes, have we any assurance that the cost to the taxpayer will be less? It will merely mean that the money will be taken from him by the federal authority, paid into the national. treasury, and returned to the provinces.
Is that necessary? If the federal authority is raising more money or is bringing into the treasury more money than it finds necessary for purely federal matters, I would suggest either that they relinquish their tax fields to the provinces or reduce certain direct taxation which will leave the individual taxpayer with a little more money with which he can pay his land or property taxes. The fact that the people in the municipalities are going to be responsible for the raising of the money which they spend on schools is a natural deterrent in the matter of the ways in which they carry out these

Education
responsibilities. They claim now-and possibly with truth-that they cannot raise enough money by taxing property and land. However, if the federal authority were to leave just a little bit more money in the hands of the property owners, through a reduction in taxation, there is no reason why the municipal authorities cannot increase their mill rate and obtain more money in that way. As I say, however, they are deterred, because they know it is a tax which appears on their statements from year to year and they find it hard, possibly, to raise it. As I say, there is a certain curb there and we can be assured that money will not be spent too recklessly in any of these ways.
The hon. member who introduced this resolution suggested that the reason given by the government for not putting forward a proposal for federal aid to education was that there would be a dominion-provincial conference. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) asks some questions of the minister; I presume it is the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), as we have no minister of education at this time and presumably we shall not need one unless we carry out the suggestions that have been brought forward from time to time by the opposition. As reported at page 472 of Hansard he asked the Prime Minister these questions:
Were any suggestions put forth by the federal or provincial governments? Is the government in favour of or opposed to federal support for elementary, secondary and university education?
That indicates that it is his intention that this resolution will go down to the very basis of our education, to grade I. In reading over the minutes of that meeting-I may be wrong; I have not had time to go through it all again-I do not recall that any provincial premier asked directly for federal aid to education. I hope-and I feel quite confident that this is so-that our Prime Minister did not search and try to find ways in which he could spend more money out of the federal treasury by offering assistance to the premiers with regard to their various problems. I do not think that was expected of him, and I am quite sure he did not do so. If he were looking for ways of disposing of the funds in the federal treasury, I am sure he would not have the confidence that he now enjoys.
The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) who introduced this resolution gave us one reason why some members oppose it:
One argument that I have heard raised is the fear of the provinces that the federal government will begin to meddle with education in the provinces if it supports general education. I fail to see any
[Mr. Byrne.)
validity in that argument. Through the war years the government co-operated with the provinces in numerous educational enterprises.
And so on.

As I said, Mr. Speaker, I believe that education is of primary importance. I do not see how we can at this time increase the possibilities for young people to obtain more education by simply granting assistance to the provincial authorities. The hon. member for Saskatoon who introduced this resolution also stated, as reported at page 463 of Hansard:
But I believe that co-operation between the dominion government and the provincial governments can bring about now some measure of that for which I speak, and we shall all be looking forward to the day when, quite irrespective of marking or tagging funds for any particular purpose, there will be an equitable arrangement in Canada for the distribution of public funds.
That possibly is a desirable situation. By "public funds" I presume he means funds

from the national treasury. That statement would indicate that the hon. member for Saskatoon feels that the federal authority should become a collecting agency to hand money to what, in my opinion, in some cases may be irresponsible provincial authorities.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in reply to the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Byrne). I have been amazed to hear the declarations made by him, particularly as to the situation in British Columbia with respect to our municipalities. I am surprised that the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) or the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mott) or both have not risen in their places to expound to you the truth regarding education in our province. speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I have already spoken once. I should be delighted to answer the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne).

speechtext:
This suggested resolution deals with assistance to the provinces. I would go further. I would like to see tagged onto it the proviso that the bulk of the money should be earmarked for the use of the municipalities. I feel that, in British Columbia particularly, we have a problem that is probably greater than that of any of the other provinces in Canada, because of the rapid growth of the population of that province in the last ten years. Both our climate and other physical conditions of the province have brought numerous people to that part of the country rather than settling on the flat lands of the prairies, with the result that our school needs have exactly doubled in the last ten years. The different districts have formed themselves into what are known as school districts in order to consolidate the educational facilities in the area.
They have made a marvellous job of consolidating. In British Columbia today we have possibly the best schools on the North American continent. This state of affairs has come about through the excellent work done by the board of education in its consolidating program. The schools that we are building are modernized; their equipment is modern, and the teachers' standards are far improved over what they were ten or twenty years ago; but we are still trying to finance our modern education by the horse and buggy method of the red school era of financing. That is, we are trying to finance basically
Education
from the land. It is true that was the best method, and possibly the logical one, years ago when land was considered the basis of wealth. But land is no longer considered the basis of wealth. Bonds, stocks, shares and other valuables have replaced land as the basis. Therefore, we should reconsider whether land is a sound basis for levying taxes for any purposes, especially for education. It has no relation to the ability of the owner of the land to pay. It bears no relation to the earning capacity of that piece of land to produce revenue to pay, and is a cause of constant discontent in every province in Canada on the part of the farmer, the home owner, and the land owner who must bear the cost of education.
Some municipalities in our province-and I take it to be true all across Canada-find that from 50 per cent to 75 per cent of their imposed taxes are levied for school purposes, leaving a very small percentage of the levied taxes to carry on other work such as road work, improvements, sidewalks, development works, water works, and so on, so that municipalities are very hard pressed.
The last speaker suggested they could raise the mill rate. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the municipalities of British Columbia have not only raised the mill rate in many cases to the limit allowed by law, but they have also increased the assessed values of the properties so taxed, so that the people cannot bear the burden much longer.
In the first place, for the reasons I have expounded, I do not believe that a tax on land for education is a fair one. The only taxes that should be a direct charge on land are those charges such as roads, supplying that land with access, sidewalks, sewers, water mains, light and so on. The direct charges on land should be those services rendered to that land, and not something negative, as far as land is concerned, such as education. But I am afraid that those school taxes on land will remain until the federal government comes to the assistance of the various provinces.
I hold in my hand a copy of Saturday Night of January 30 which contains an article written by a gentleman who I understand is a teacher. His name is Percy J. Kennedy. He has given a good summing up of the situation so far as my point of view is concerned. Not only are the municipalities hard pressed and incapable of meeting their obligations to the full, but they are suffering, as a result, as are our whole educational systems, plus the personnel who are carrying on a notable work

Education
in educating our children. I should like to quote from this article as follows:
Taxation levied on property assessment only, for school purposes, is no longer adequate. Glaring inequalities in educational opportunity exist among the provinces and between different parts of the same province and municipality.
These inequalities result from differences in taxpaying ability, wealth, income, and the relative number of children to be educated.
Not only have the provinces very unequal abilities to support education, but also they have very unequal educational burdens. The poorer provinces have more children in proportion to the adult population. Consequently, the poorer provinces and communities make a proportionately much greater financial effort to pay for schools than the richer ones. In spite of this greater effort, the results are totally inadequate and are reflected in poorly-trained teachers, low salaries, barren curricula, and wretched school buildings. This situation is illustrated by some pertinent facts contained in a brief submitted to the dominion government by the Canadian Teachers' Federation in February, 1949.
I quote from the brief:
(a)	One out of every ten teachers in Canada holds only a permit or temporary certificate.
(b)	The average salary of rural teachers throughout Canada is $1,207 per annum while urban teachers' salaries average $2,120. (These figures do not include Quebec or Newfoundland.)
(c)	The median teachers' salaries for the year 1947 range from $816 in Prince Edward Island to $2,042 in British Columbia.
(d)	At the end of 1947 there were 1,700 fewer teachers in Canada than there were in 1939.
(e)	In April, 1948, approximately 22,000 pupils in two provinces were receiving their education through correspondence courses because of the lack of teachers.
One of the standard arguments against federal aid for education is "Where are we going to get the money?" Well, in these days of billions for armaments and widespread public spending for other purposes, it would be strange indeed if the federal government could not provide the relatively small amount needed.
I would recommend the complete article to any hon. member who is interested enough to read it later on. I entirely agree with the article. I	agree	that if	you want to getteachers of a	high	calibre	in	the teaching[DOT]profession you	have	to pay	the	price. While$2,000 sounds	high	in British	Columbia, a
man with the qualifications of a teacher, the holder of a B.A., an M.A. or some other degree could easily go into industry and get three times that amount for possibly easier and steadier work and a better pension.
Yesterday, the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) mentioned that 130,000 veterans had been taught through government assistance since the last war. He commended the effort of the government in that regard. I also commend it. I think the government did an excellent job in training the returned men through these university courses, but I also reflect this way: If the. incidence of war and its conclusion discloses the fact that we

have 130,000 young men thirsting for knowledge and capable of absorbing it, and the government recognizes that fact and gives them facilities to acquire that knowledge, it is a splendid thing. But the government's policy of assistance ends immediately when the veteran has completed his education, and the excellent idea involved in training our youth and giving them a higher education is lost sight of. My case is that we have the same thirst for knowledge from approximately an equal number of young men and women in peace as we had in war, and we should take the same care and accept the same responsibility for having them sent to our universities. However, in this instance they meet with frustration because they have not the means to carry on their ambition to enter university life.
It may be said that our universities are not capable of taking care of any more than they have at the present time. I would draw attention to the fact that in British Columbia we had a university capable of taking care of only 3,500 students; but immediately students were available and the need was there the funds were available, and in a few months the university increased its capacity so as to take care of 8,000 veterans and to give them a first-class education. The same can be done in peacetime, if the need is there- and I know it is there-if the wherewithal is given by the federal government to meet the cost of this type of education. This will make not only fine students but eventually much finer citizens of those young people who can absorb that education.
There is no legal barrier. I believe the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) made it quite clear that the legal barrier is nonexistent. It was overcome in the case of the veterans and in the case of technical schools, and in connection with other assistance already rendered by the government.
I can assure the house that any type of aid in any form, whether to the junior classes or to the universities, will be welcomed across the country. It will be welcomed not only by those people who will receive the benefit of that help, but by every land owner in the whole dominion whether in urban or rural areas. I am not suggesting how much should be given, or in what way, but I do ask the government sincerely not to turn the bill down but to accept the challenge it offers. It asks the government only to consider the subject, and I think that the least the government can do is to accept that challenge on behalf of its young citizens, whom they recognized immediately after the war and have proceeded to forget in peacetime.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to make any extended remarks at this stage. May I first express my sympathy with the resolution. No province in Canada has contributed more to education in proportion to its resources than has Nova Scotia. Nearly one hundred years ago Sir Charles Tupper established free schools there. For a time it was a serious political problem. Many families who had educated their members privately were taxed so that others might become educated. Even to this day we see in families of Nova Scotia political sympathies which originated at that time.
For many years education in Nova Scotia was at a low ebb. I recall that in 1925 school teachers' salaries were as low as $300 a year. They accepted teaching positions only for a short time so that they could get better positions later or until they were married.
Standards in the teaching profession have been greatly improved, and the teachers require higher relative salaries so that they may make teaching their life?s work. In 1925 and thereafter not only were the salaries low but the standards of education were low, and no pension fund was available. Having regard to the limited revenues of Nova Scotia, large contributions have been made to education.
Nova Scotia has taken pride in the educating of its families, but unfortunately for us many who have received the benefits of that education go to other provinces and other countries, at the expense of their native province.
In the early days of confederation Nova Scotia contributed its part toward acquiring the lands in western Canada where certain sections of each township were set aside for educational purposes. However no school benefits came to our provinces.
While teachers' salaries have increased to a considerable extent in recent years, living costs have increased in greater proportion. Because those who enter the teaching profession must spend such a long time securing the required qualifications, if they intend to make teaching their life's work, they are entitled to payment on that basis.
I do not intend to take up more time in a discussion of the motion, but I must state that I am in complete sympathy with the purpose of it. Anything we can do to assist education and our teachers should be done. Many of them are carrying on at great personal sacrifice. Some hon. members have pointed out that members of the teaching profession have felt it their duty to make sacrifices by way of salaries in order that they might continue teaching. Taxation on lands and property for educational purposes

Mr. Speaker, we have listened with keen interest to the discussion on a resolution that comes before the house not for the first time. Without in any way detracting from its high calibre, as one listened to this debate I am sure one could not help thinking that many of the arguments heard before in favour of the resolution have been repeated on this occasion.
If I may say so, I believe most of the speeches have dealt with the subject in such a way as to win wide acceptance in every section of the house. For instance, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdon-nell) made a passionate plea for the adoption of the resolution, if western civilization, as it is called, is to be preserved. Other hon. members have pointed out the low incomes received by teachers. Many have said that because of the near-saturation point in taxation on real estate, which is fundamental in the provision of resources for education in various communities throughout the country,
. municipal governments find difficulty with this problem.
With all of that, and with much more that has been said, I am sure every one of us in the house is in full accord. No one will deny the importance of education, particularly its importance in maintaining the proper functioning of a democratic country or democratic society. No one will deny the importance of education. One recognizes too, as the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) has said, that the great battle of ideologies that is now on in the world will in the final analysis be won not by arms alone but by the attitude of the peoples of the world towards the validity of those ideologies. There education will play its great role. With all of that I am sure no one need spend much time in insisting that we are in full agreement.
What we have to decide is not whether education is a valuable thing but what is the best way in this federal state of ours to see that we have the best of education and that our citizens, our children, rich and poor alike, are given the best opportunities to enjoy the heritage which comes from a good educational system. That is the problem. Since in my judgment that is the problem before us at the moment, I would invite the house to consider again the terms of the resolution before us, which reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration means of expanding

Education
and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada, by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose.
We have to face this resolution in the light not of what we would like it to mean but of what it actually says. It calls for a program which I shall endeavour to show is not within the competence of this parliament. It calls for a program that in no way can be said to be opposed by those who take issue with this motion. We on this side of the house who take that position do so because we regard the adoption of this particular motion at this particular time in this federal state of ours as one that would be calculated to hinder the progress of education and educational opportunity rather than to further it.
Before stating the two main arguments I wish to offer, may I say that we have yet to hear from the Massey commission. I do not know exactly when that report will be brought in, but I imagine the time is not far distant. While I presume that the report will not deal with all the aspects of education envisaged by this particular resolution, I think one may reasonably expect that it will deal with a number of matters that are germane to the resolution under discussion.
That commission has had the opportunity of listening to representations by all sorts of bodies, educationists, provincial authorities, voluntary associations in this field, labour Organizations and the like. The commission carried its sittings into every one of our ten provinces. I submit that before we make hasty judgment it would be well for us to await the recommendations which that commission will make.
It was suggested the other day that one of the reasons I had given last year why we should not consider a similar resolution was that a dominion-provincial conference was to be held, and that since this was a matter that clearly came within the competence of the provincial authorities we should await their views, which presumably might be expressed at that conference. The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) took me to task in the speech he made the other day. All I have to say in defence is that when the conference did take place on December 4 no province raised that question. Undoubtedly, if they had desired to do so, they were influenced largely, as we all were, by the seriousness of the international situation and our consequential obligations.	But the
fact is that the provinces themselves did not initiate any discussion or put forward any proposals that would deal with the matter covered by the resolution now before us.

Be that as it may, I want to emphasize as clearly as I can that we do not want to give the impression to teachers and to young men and women who wish to acquire an education but who And it difficult for financial reasons that in opposing this resolution we are not interested in the objectives which undoubtedly the proposer had in mind. Speaking on a similar resolution, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is reported on page 946 of Hansard of October 19, 1949, as follows: Personally I have no doubt that it will be necessary to find some way in which these institutions can continue to be supplied with that which is necessary to them to maintain that high standard in their educational activities.
Although we are in full sympathy with the resolution as regards the objectives which the hon. gentleman has in mind, the words of the Prime Minister indicate that we will have to devise methods. Those methods must be orderly. They must not be so created as to destroy the very purpose which I am sure the hon, gentleman had in mind.'

speechtext:
I think he was confining himself to that aspect of the problem. He was referring to the Massey commission, but what helps one phase of educational activity certainly helps another. We have to approach this question in an orderly way.
In 1941 the Sirois commission had to deal with this important matter and they went into this very problem. They listened to the representatives of the provincial governments and of other agencies throughout the country who were proposing that because of the reduction in educational expenditures by the provinces owing to the severe depression the federal government should provide some assistance to supplement the general budgetary obligations of the provinces. At page 51 of book II of the recommendations of that commission, these words appear:
It has-even been contended that the dominion is bound to see that there is equal educational opportunity (as far as is practicable) for every Canadian child. We have the deepest sympathy for these views which have been advanced by many of the organizations most closely associated with education in Canada, and we share to the full the regret that, especially in recent years, education has been terribly neglected in many of the poorer parts of the country and that wholly disproportionate sacrifices have been imposed on those who have devoted their lives to this important public service.
That represents, if I may digress for a moment, another argument that has been put forward in favour of the resolution in its present terms. Then the commission goes on: But the representations appear to us to go too far in denying the right of each province to decide

the relative importance of expenditure on education and expenditure on other competing services. It is our hope that provision can be made for the fiscal needs of all provinces, including within those needs provision for the education of the young. Our financial proposals aim at placing every province in a position to discharge its responsibilities for education (on a scale that is within the means of the people of Canada) if it chooses to do so. Once this position is established it seems to us best that education, like every other form of welfare service in a democratic community, should have to fight for its life, and that a generous provision for the education of the children of the nation should depend, not on an arbitrary constitutional provision, but on the persistent conviction of the mass of the people that they must be ready to deny themselves some of the good things of life in order to deal fairly by their children.
Then the report concludes:
Hence we do not think that it would be wise or appropriate for the dominion to make grants to the provinces earmarked for the support of general education.
I am aware that no one must accept the findings of this commission as an infallible declaration on the subject, but at least they do represent a considered view, and one to which we must pay the strictest attention in discussing this important matter. The resolution says nothing about consultation with the provinces. One would have thought that [DOT] before the resolution could reach the stage-
I was going to say of responsibility, but I will not use that word-of wide acceptance in this house, some indication should have been given as to the means by which the provinces were going to be consulted, the means by which their views could be made known and the means by which the views of the municipalities could be expressed, because through their school boards the municipalities have a tremendous stake and a tremendous interest in this problem.
It would be wrong to suggest, in answer to what I have just said, that the federal government should initiate the matter. I am sure anyone who has had responsibility, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) had when he was minister of education in Ontario, will realize the position any federal government would be in if it suggested that this government or this parliament should take a direct interest in matters which under the constitution are specifically reserved for the provinces. And it is important, irritating though it may be to some in the house who would like to see this question finally disposed of, to remember that we are citizens of a federal state, and undoubtedly it is the desire of the people of Canada that this federalism should continue in its present form. I am sure no one in this house would suggest anything else. Well, the implication in the recommendation of the Rowell-Sirois report to
*	Education
which I referred is clearly that if we are going to maintain the federal character of our state we must clearly observe the principles of action that have been envisaged for the preservation of that federalism. Section 93 of the British North America Act is of the greatest interest in trying to decide which side one should take with respect to this resolution. In the principal paragraph section 93 reads:
In and for each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to education, subject and according to the following provisions-
The ensuing provisions have no relation to the subject under discussion. The important thing is that not only have the provinces been given jurisdiction in this matter; the word "exclusively" is used, and some significance must be attached to the inclusion of that word in the section, for it is not widely or generally used throughout most of the other sections of the act. This clearly indicates that the intention was, as in fact we know it still is, that education was and, as we all believe, should be the domain of the provinces. We know the national unity of this country is predicated in very large measure upon the preservation of that constitutional fact; and any interference with it I submit would greatly impede the cause of education instead of furthering it.
During the past year, together with a number of my colleagues of the government, I had the opportunity of attending conferences with the provinces with respect to agreement on constitutional matters, as well as the conference on December 4 on wider terms of reference. Anyone who has followed those proceedings will realize, I think, how sacrosanct, not only in legal fact but in desire, is this competence given the provinces regarded by provincial governments at the present time. For that reason among others we must take issue with and oppose this resolution.
Some may say that we are already assisting education in a specific manner for a specific purpose. That is true, and I propose to deal with that point in some detail. Before doing so, however, let us look at the terms of this resolution again. It does not call upon the federal government to provide moneys to assist for a particular purpose. It calls upon the federal government to provide financial assistance so that we may expand and equalize educational opportunity across Canada. In other words its purposes are general, for general education. No one would argue successfully, I am sure, that you could expand or equalize educational opportunity without going into the whole matter of educational policy; and I submit with great confidence it would be a most serious mistake to argue

Education
that we should pass a resolution which so obviously, on the face of it, is not within our competence. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr, Gillis) said this was an important matter; that it was important that we should expand and equalize educational opportunity, and that right here and now in this house we should amend the constitution if that is a stumbling block. Well, I have great respect for the hon. member, but I am sure that upon reflection he will see how impracticable his suggestion is. He will see the position in which we would be placed, not only as a government but as a parliament, by passing a resolution which would require as an initial step the amendment of the constitution in a particular which the fathers of confederation intended should be reserved exclusively to the provinces and which present provincial governments, at least for the most part, are very jealous in seeing maintained in the division of powers as between the two senior levels of government in Canada.
Having said that, one should not get or give the impression that the federal government is not interested in supplementing educational effort in a way which brings that effort within the purview of section 93 of the British North Amerioa Act. I doubt if hon. members have given sufficient attention to one of the most effective ways, within the constitution, of providing the means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada. We are doing that now in a constitutional way through family allowances. We have put at the disposal of parents, as trustees for over four million children, moneys by which, among other things, the opportunities of education have been more readily granted and secured than at any time in our history. If one really wanted to find a measure that was constitutional, and that did provide the means for expanding and equalizing educational opportunity, one could see it in the Family Allowances Act itself. I am sure the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) will agree with me when I say that, as a result of the passage of the family allowances measure, the school attendance record in all of our provinces, not less so than in the province of Ontario, has been strengthened and has reached a peak never exceeded before. This is due simply to the fact that, in so far as the education of children until the age of sixteen is concerned, the parents do not draw family allowances unless the children complete the statutory period at school.
I submit that in calculating what we are doing to assist education in the constitutional way afforded us we have in the family allowances measure the most effective means
rMr. Martin.]
of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity in Canada. But that is by no means the full story of what we are doing here through the federal government to make it possible, for specific purposes coming within the ambit of the constitution, to expand and increase educational opportunity. I have calculated that, in addition to family allowances, the federal government is spending now about $35 million a year in the field of education, apart from educational courses that are connected in some way with the training of the armed forces. In the federal programs nothing has heretofore been done for the purpose of formulating policy or dealing with basic fundamentals of education in any province. We have simply provided grants for specific purposes that conform precisely with the policies already formulated by the provinces in the field of education. Under the decisions of our courts such acts are constitutional for the simple reason they do not seek to intervene in a field over which we have no legislative competence.
We have various measures. I start with one that, perhaps in terms of full effect, is not as great as some other measures, but it is a significant contribution. I refer to the grants we make to nine of the ten provinces, amounting to about $3 million a year, that are extended under the Vocational Training Coordination Act for youth training, apprenticeship training, vocational school assistance and so forth. Hon. members will recall that at the end of the last war a program of assistance to technical schools in Canada was arranged. This program had a ten-year duration. While it has not been carried on since, it has been carried on in another way through the grant that I have just mentioned, and through others to which I shall refer later.
The grants made for youth training under this act include, for instance, student scholarships under federal-provincial agreement. Then, we have an expenditure of around $2 million a year to provide for payment to the provinces for capital expenditures for vocational school buildings and equipment.
Another indirect but important contribution is that made by the federal government arising out of the fiscal agreements that were entered into in 1945, and the fiscal agreement which it is anticipated will be entered into this year. Assuming full agreement with the offer made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to the provinces last December, the provinces will be given by the federal government over $300 million a year to enable them to supplement their own resources and carry out projects and work which, under the constitution, are given to the provinces.

Now, of the $100 million, for instance, that was offered to the province of Ontario under the agreement proposed by the Minister of Finance in December, undoubtedly a good portion would go to bolster up the exchequer of the department of education of that province. I believe that in a federal state, where you want to preserve the true federal character of that state, one of the best ways for doing this is to let the provinces decide what portion of the moneys under their control shall be spent for a particular purpose. If we want to destroy the character of federalism in this country, and I know that none of us do, all we have to do is to say to the provinces that we are willing to give them so much money, but that money must be spent for a particular purpose, to wit for educational purposes. Out of the $100 million, let us say, in the case to which I have just referred, we would say so much is for education, provided you adopt a certain program in respect of education. How long would the cordial relationship between the two levels of government prevail in Canada if those conditions were attached to the moneys paid, under fiscal agreement or otherwise, by the federal government?
Then one should not forget the grants made, for instance, for schools of social work to which the member for Eglinton referred. He expressed the hope that such a worthy project would find additional support in the estimates this year. One will have to wait and see what happens in that regard, but I may say to him that I am very hopeful there will be an increase in that amount.
