But that is an important contribution made to education by the federal government in the only way we have the legal power to do it, to give this money, in this particular instance to the university for a particular purpose and not for the kind of general purpose, laudable as that general purpose may be, as is envisaged in the resolution we are now discussing.
Under the national health program, projects providing for the training of health personnel will call for the expenditure of more than $2 million during this fiscal year. Hon. members may be interested in knowing that under that program up to this period over three thousand five- hundred individuals have received financial assistance to enable them to obtain training in various fields of health activities. No one will for a moment deny the importance of that contribution, but it is important to recognize that the contribution is being made for a specific purpose by a government that is charged with not being interested in seeing
Education
that there is an expansion and an equalization of educational opportunity in Canada. Thousands of dollars are being spent through grants made directly to the provinces for the purchase of teaching equipment, the purchase of films, the purchase of projectors that are being used in schools; the purchase of all sorts of modern equipment which it is thought brings home more aptly than otherwise, and more efficiently than formerly, the subjects taught in our schools and in our universities. I do not have the exact amount of money that has been provided by the federal government for equipment.
A large part of the funds under the national health grants is going to institutions of higher learning through the federal grants for research. Last year when the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) spoke on this matter, he referred to the importance of research; and I agree fully with what he said. But just think of the tremendous expansion that has taken place in the amount of money which the federal government is now making available to various bodies for research in this country. In the field of medicine alone, the amount of money has increased to more than one million dollars. That covers grants to universities and grants that are made by the national research council for purposes somewhat analogous to the one I have just mentioned. That is assistance to education. It is perhaps not assistance to every boy and girl but it is assistance made to education and in the only way in which the federal government can, constitutionally, give assistance.
Again, under the national health grants program, nearly $300,000 has been committed this year, for instance, to assist Canadian universities in research. This is a project of great significance, in that it involves research workers from every province making a coordinated scientific attack on health problems.
Then there are the funds that we provide for Indian education and grants for residential schools for Indians, which amount to more than $6 million a year. While the outlays on veterans educational training has declined from its post-war peak, in the last fiscal year close to $19 million was expended in the form of allowances, tuition and fees, and supplementary grants for vocational and university training. Large sums of money are being spent on training by the Department of National Defence. While it is true that money is for the training of members of the armed services, nevertheless they are Canadians to whom I am sure would apply

Education
the reference made in the resolution to educational opportunity. One could go on reciting the federal contribution that is being made to the provinces, in a constitutional way, in order to strengthen education in this country.
For the reasons that I have given we cannot support this resolution. No one has better expressed our point of view than has the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) himself when he spoke in this house on October 19, 1949. His words are to be found at page 946, volume 1 of Hansard, second session, for that year. He said:
I am sure all hon. members have welcomed this opportunity of focusing their attention upon this assertion . . . that there should be across Canada the greatest possible degree of equality of opportunity for the education of our young Canadians, the Canadians of the next generation.
Whether or not the granting of financial assistance by the federal government to the various provinces could be arranged in such a manner as to avoid exercising any direct or indirect control over the field of education, which is essentially within provincial jurisdiction, is a question offering greater possibilities of controversy.
There is no doubt that every one of us, as a Canadian citizen, is vitally concerned with the necessity of there being maintained in this country adequate educational facilities to produce the kind of citizens who may be able to make the best possible use of the bountiful resources with which Providence has blessed our great country. And there can be no doubt that, since the cessation of hostilities, the program devised to provide educational facilities for veterans of war has been of great assistance in the maintenance of the efficiency of our educational institutions. I think many of us feel that, without the assistance it was possible to provide during that period, many of our institutions would have found it very difficult indeed to maintain their activities to the high degree which is so satisfactory to the Canadian public.
Personally I have no doubt that it will be necessary to find some way in which these institutions can continue to be supplied with that which is necessary to them to maintain that high standard in their educational activities.
That statement I am sure represents the feeling of all of us. We all want to see the objectives of this resolution carried out; but those of us with responsibility in government at the moment must take the position: What is the most effective way by which that objective can be achieved? We feel that it can best be achieved in the way that we are doing it now, constitutionally, namely by giving assistance for specific purposes, not in any way in opposition to declared policy of education in any one of our ten provinces. The only other way would be by doing what the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) suggested but which, as I said a moment ago, I am sure he would, on further consideration admit was an impractical solution. Therefore in opposing this resolution we would not want anyone in this house or in the country to think that we do

not recognize the need for and the desirability of giving to every child in this country the best possible opportunity for education in accordance with her or his talent. But we believe the way to bring that about is to do it within the terms of the constitution, in that way preserving the cause of federalism as we understand it in Canada and in that way more effectively promoting the cause of education. We believe it is better to do it in that way than by following a suggestion which cannot be accepted because it is a matter wholly within the competence of another legislative authority and alien to our own.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EQUALIZING OF OPPORTUNITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there seems to be general agreement with regard to the importance of education and with regard to the desirability of respecting the constitutional basis upon which the educational systems of this country have proceeded for so many years. Having said that, I must say that 1 find it difficult to follow the reasoning of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), who has just taken his seat, in connection with some of the points he has put forward. He emphasized the fact that it would be most undesirable that there should be any interference with the constitutional authority of the provinces in the field of education. I have already expressed myself so vigorously on the subject that I certainly would have no thought now of expressing any other opinion. I have been a strong advocate of the exclusive jurisdiction of the [DOT]provinces in the field of education, for historical and other reasons. I can think of nothing that would be so likely to disturb the friendly relationship between the various governments of this country as to seek, directly or indirectly, to interfere with the authority of the provincial governments over a field which, for many obvious reasons, is regarded jealously as their exclusive right and responsibility.
I would point out, however, that ways have been found of assisting in different fields, including the field of education, without in any way interfering with the division of constitutional responsibility. I do not wish to labour the subject because it has been referred to several times, but I do think that the reference that has already been made to the extremely satisfactory co-operation between the dominion and the provincial governments in the education of veterans of the last war is something that might well be remembered by Canadians in the years ahead.
As has been pointed out, more than 130,000 Canadian veterans received education in the higher levels, and without exception that met with the satisfaction and approval of the

veterans themselves as well as the general public. In that instance the dominion government provided the money for the education, and the educational program and the actual administration of the education itself were carried out entirely by the departments of education of the different provinces under a comparatively simple and workable agreement between the Department of Labour and the department of education of each of the provincial governments. That form of education carried on through the war years and afterwards in a very satisfactory way. There are other examples of co-operation of that kind.
The minister who has just spoken is one who has reason to know that these exclusive fields do not always present the constitutional barriers where there is an attempt or where there is a definite plan to assist in a particular way. Having said that, I concede that many of the things he has mentioned, which are being handled by the dominion government, contribute their share to the general opportunity for education in this country from the financial point of view. But I would point out that just as education is the exclusive field of jurisdiction of the provincial governments so is hospitalization, except for marine hospitalization. Nevertheless, no insuperable barrier has been encountered by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) in finding a way to assist the hospitals of this country, and hospitalization generally, where it was found that the provincial governments did have some difficulty in that field. I would, point out to those who are interested in the strictly constitutional aspect that section 92, subsection 7, brings under the exclusive power of the provincial legislatures the establishment, maintenance, and management of hospitals, asylums, charities, and eleemosynary institutions in and for the province, other than marine hospitals. We have had evidence of the fact that plans could be made under which assistance could be given in some of these exclusive fields which do not invade the jurisdiction and authority of the provinces.
I would go further. These plans have been carried forward in many instances without any suggestion that directly or indirectly there was interference with the administrative responsibilities of these provincial departments which handle these particular activities. Having said that, I would point out that no matter what measure of assistance there may be to the public through these various contributions, which are being made by the dominion government in the many fields already mentioned by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the inescapable fact remains that from one side of this
Education
country to the other university presidents, those responsible for university and college education, as well as representatives of school boards, and municipal authorities are making the emphatic statement that they simply cannot carry on under the situation which exists today, with the mounting costs and with the legitimate demands of professors and teachers for higher pay in the face of the increasing cost of living.
That is the situation with which we are confronted. Whether it is true of every province or not, there can be no doubt about the fact that a number of the provinces are not in a financial position today to meet these added demands. Whether this subject was specifically discussed at the last dominion-provincial conference or not, the fact remains that this is a problem which is very much in the mind of each of the provincial governments. They have no opportunity to forget it. They are being pressed by universities, colleges, technical institutions, school boards, municipal councils and others for further assistance in this field so that they may meet the increasing cost of education in these institutions and in the various communities.
The minister has stated that this would mean the entry of the federal government into the field of education. I for one would argue very strongly against any such invasion. That is one reason why I do not agree that direct grants by the dominion government to universities or other institutions would be an extremely difficult problem, and one which could only create grave difficulties in many instances. Unless there were some department of government here in Ottawa which was in a position to examine the qualifications and standards of each of these institutions the government would hardly be in a position to determine what grants it should or should not make. For that reason I am satisfied that in that case as in other cases it would be well to leave the responsi-oility for education in the hands of the departments of education of the different provinces.
However, I do not read the resolution now before us in the same limited way in which the minister has read it. When I use the expression "same limited way" I do not mean that there is any limitation in his capacity to read it, but rather that he has placed a limitation upon its meaning which I do not see in the actual wording of the resolution. I think that when we read that there should be "financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose" we can take that as meaning that this would be

Education
under some arrangement agreeable to the provinces whereby some measure of equalization would take place; so that those provinces which today are less fortunate from the financial point of view than others would have some measure of equalization, and so that they could extend opportunities in the field of education comparable to those afforded by any other province.
Each province in this country is not equally capable of meeting these responsibilities, from the financial point of view. That is no reflection on any province which finds itself in that position. Because of a smaller percentage of industrial and mercantile activity, the maritime provinces undoubtedly would find it more difficult to meet these responsibilities. Newfoundland, our newest province, also will have great difficulty in bringing up its educational standards, unless it receives some special assistance that will make it possible to equalize opportunities in that province, or to bring them to a point where they will compare favourably with those in the more highly industrialized parts of the country.
Without going into further detail I would go back to the Rowell-Sirois report, to which the minister has referred. The Rowell-Sirois report did suggest that it was not desirable that grants be specifically earmarked; and in doing so it recognized the fact that indirectly the dominion government could exercise influence over education if that were done. This was not considered desirable; it was resisted strongly by most of the provinces at that time, and would be resisted just as strongly today,
But then the Rowell-Sirois report went on to say and to recommend that there should be made available a fund which would be allocated to those provinces with a financial capacity to meet this and other similar obligations which was not as great as the financial capacity of the provinces with greater revenue opportunities. The recommendation for the creation of such a fund was put forward at the dominion-provincial conference in 1945. The term which I believe was used in the Rowell-Sirois recommendation, and also at the conference, was that such a fund should be used for the purpose of making grants in aid to those provinces which needed additional financial resources for these purposes.
It may be that a fund of that kind which, after all, would be made available from the general revenue of the country and which, because of that very fact, would draw more heavily from those provinces with the highest revenues, would meet a situation of this kind. I do not think the resolution now
before us in any way precludes full examination of such a plan, and I have not heard any suggestion made in arguments supporting the resolution that any such plan which would be acceptable to the provinces would not be contemplated by the resolution, which simply asks that those steps be taken which will equalize educational opportunities across Canada.
I do think we should do everything we can to equalize educational opportunity. Democracy is perhaps facing its greatest dangers at this time. Democracy is based upon the principle of equality. There is no single thing which will assure equality to as great an extent as will education. A child with no financial advantages, but who receives the best educational opportunity, can go forth into life with the greatest measure of equality any state can give.
We have in Canada primary, secondary, college, technical and university education, all of which are part of the educational systems of the country. It seems to me the target at which we should aim is to make sure that every child of every race or creed, and from every part of the country, no matter what the financial circumstances of that child's parents may be, shall be able to advance through every stage of our educational system, dependent only upon the ability, the capacity and the initiative of the child concerned. That target, that goal, may be difficult to attain; but it seems to me that is the goal. It seems to me that is the thing toward which we should all be striving.
We do know that when the opportunity was afforded the veterans to take college, technical and university education, many young men and women took that education who never could have taken it if the facilities had not been provided as one of the options offered to them after the last war. I commend the government for what it did in that respect. I am sure no investment was ever better made and no money ever better spent than that which gave to the young men and women education to equalize their opportunity for the years ahead. It did more than anything else could have done.
It seems to me that should be the ideal toward which we should all work. There are distant parts of the country where special arrangements will have to be made. The less developed those areas are, the greater the task will be and the more heavily the cost will fall on those very provinces least capable financially of meeting the extra burden.
It is for that very reason that I would not advocate any uniform system of grants which would provide the same amount for the

children from every province of this country, because I recognize the fact that there are provinces in Canada which have great financial advantages, and that what we need is an equalization which would make it possible in those provinces with more limited financial resources to carry forward education to the very highest level, where children are able to avail themselves of that education.
There is plenty of evidence of the increasing interest in higher education. Different members have spoken, and properly, with some measure of pride and some measure of advocacy, in regard to the universities in which they were interested. We have within a very short distance of the House of Commons one of the new and growing universities, which stands as a demonstration of how rapidly interest in higher education is increasing today. Carleton college, located not far from where we are now, opened its first classes in June of 1942. In its last school year it had an enrolment of 1,570 pupils who received a very advanced type of education in the general line of arts and also in such specialized lines as journalism and business administration, which it seems to me is particularly appropriate in an institution reasonably close to the seat of government. Carleton college is not only demonstrating its own vitality and vigour, which commands the respect not only of this community but of the whole country; it is demonstrating the great interest on the part of young people of this country in that higher education which is made available to them by the new institutions which are opening up in this way.
While I have some personal interest in other institutions and while I respect the antiquity of the universities referred to by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) and by the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), as well as by other hon. members who have spoken, I think we should have regard to the new universities which are extending opportunities in areas where those opportunities have not previously been presented.
I should like to refer to another point made by the minister who has spoken. He left the impression that in reaching a decision on this subject the government was waiting for the report of the Massey commission. I must confess that I am wholly unable to see what subject in the terms of reference of the Massey commission has the slightest bearing on this resolution. The Massey commission was given four general terms of reference. One was to inquire into the principles which should guide Canadian policy in radio and television. Another was to make recommendations as to the policy to be followed by agencies of the government, such as the 80709-381
Education
national film board, national gallery, national museum and agencies of that kind. The next was the methods by which relations could be carried on with the United Nations educational, scientific and cultural organizations and similar organizations of that nature. The fourth was the relations of the governmen' of Canada with various national voluntary bodies. It does not seem to me that any of those terms of reference embrace the subject matter of this resolution.
I should like to point out a matter that has been referred to in the earlier discussions. I believe this is a subject of great urgency. Even at this time I urge the government to reconsider its decision simply to vote against this resolution and by doing so to defer any action in regard to this problem which has emerged and which must be dealt with unless education in this country is going to be restricted seriously in many fields. I would ask them to recognize that our primary and secondary school systems, our technical schools, our colleges and our universities are all suffering from the fact that our teachers are not today generally receiving a financial return which is in any way comparable to the education they must possess in the first place and the effort they must put into the important task which is before them.
In saying this I know I am not saying anything with which the minister or any members on the opposite side of the house will disagree. I wish, however, to emphasize the urgency of this problem. Teachers are not just people of another occupation. I hope I shall be pardoned for repeating something I said in this house on an earlier occasion. I believe that next to the ministry itself-I am talking now about the ministry in the churches-there is no higher calling to which men and women may devote their service than the calling which is going to guide the destiny of this country through the moulding of the character of our youth. To an extent that we seem so reluctant to recognize, the whole future of this country, the standard of life of the people iif the days ahead, will depend very largely upon the character and also upon the spirit and the measure of personal confidence which our teachers have in their own future. That will in itself impart something to the children, whether they intend to impart that spirit or not.
I shall refer once again to words of mine which were quoted this afternoon. We can build the most magnificent structures that any nation ever built to house its educational activities, but that will be of little avail unless

Education
the education of the teachers and the spirit in which they carry on their work are such as to develop in the youth of Canada not only higher character but also that confidence which will give to them the vitality and initiative which are so essential in a nation with such challenging opportunities as we possess in Canada today.
I want also to point out, Mr. Speaker, that while we are confronted with heavy costs, which none of us must ignore, there are some aspects of education which can compensate somewhat for the dollars that are spent. I am sure that every dollar spent on providing a really good education will be a dollar saved in our prisons, our reform institutions and the various corrective establishments across this country. Even if you cannot measure it in actual dollar savings in these very costly institutions, we can see the value that will be gained in what might be regarded as the capital investment in skill and character of our people.
Then there is the value of health itself. There is an old Latin maxim, mens sana in corpore sano. A healthy mind may naturally be in a healthy body. Also I think that a healthy mind will contribute greatly to the development of a healthy body. I feel sure that no one will support me more vigorously in that than the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor). After all, there is no provision for health which will have more effect than to instil in the minds of our youth a healthy respect for their own bodies, a healthy mental discipline which will guide their course of action, and some acceptance of those standards of life which in themselves will most effectively protect them against many of the infirmities and many of the dangers which all of us must encounter in this complex society of ours.
Now before I conclude my remarks I want to refer to just one other statement that was made this afternoon. I must confess some surprise at the statement by one hon. member that he would be very greatly concerned about a system that wopld pass on additional money to irresponsible local bodies. Our whole educational system right across Canada, in every one of the provinces, is based upon the idea of local authority in intimate contact with the local problems of the people themselves. I believe one of the most disastrous things that could happen would be to try to direct educational activities from some central point, where these human contacts would be broken and it would become something like an industrial production line.
IMr. Drew.]

Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not
think the hon. member has improved the situation very much by his remark. I thought he had said local authorities, but if he says he said provincial authorities I certainly accept that statement. In that case I would express even greater concern, because these are the authorities that guide the educational system of this country, and which the minister has been emphasizing must continue to guide it.
Without enlarging upon this further, Mr. Speaker, I believe we do not need to examine too closely the precise wording of the resolution and ask ourselves whether we would like to change it a little. What is the purpose of this resolution? The purpose is to emphasize the need for an immediate attempt to meet what has already become an urgent situation. The urgency of that situation is being emphasized by municipal authorities, by college authorities, by representatives of universities and by people generally across Canada. I believe our target should be to equalize educational opportunities so that every child may really have a chance to go as far as that child's mental capacity makes possible; and I believe passing this resolution would emphasize our belief that this should be done. The government could then sit down with the provincial authorities and lay plans for an equalization of opportunity which does not exist today.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since my colleague and I, in common with many other members in this house, have received representations from the various organizations concerning federal government support for education, I feel that I should make a few remarks at this time. We have received messages from three of the most prominent organizations in Newfoundland, the Newfoundland teachers' association, the Newfoundland federation of labour, and the Canadian Legion, Newfoundland command. I have reason to know something of the work of the teachers in Newfoundland, and I believe there is no finer body of men and women in the country. Because of the geography of the country they often have to undergo severe hardships and make great sacrifices in carrying on their profession for

a small remuneration. It has often been said that the salaries received by teachers do not compare with those received by people in the lowest class of labour.
This afternoon the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) delivered an interesting speech in which he summarized all the arguments that were used, and stated that most members in the house were in agreement that education was the sort of thing they could all support. He expressed the view that the government was sympathetic with the idea which the sponsor of this resolution has brought forward. Then he laid down two grounds of objection: first, that it was not within the competence of the federal government to give assistance; second, that it was calculated to hinder rather than to help education. He gave no arguments that I can recall to support this latter ground, but he did argue that it was not within the competence of the federal government to give this assistance to education.
He stated first of all that during the recent dominion-provincial conference in December, no province ventured to raise the question of support for education. I believe I am quoting him correctly when I say that. At the time I had in front of me the proceedings of the conference, so I looked up the index and found that the premier of Manitoba had made several remarks on the subject, and had suggested methods by which the federal government could give assistance to such worthy objects as education. The premier wound up his remarks with a list of seven principal points which he considered essential to the discussion, and the seventh one was this:
Recognition that the national interest in education, both because of its nature and its cost, has reached the point that substantial contributions from the federal treasury are required and justified to provide an adequate standard of education throughout the country.
Probably the minister had forgotten that the premier of Manitoba had made education an issue at that time. I believe that the premier of the newest province also felt that was the sort of subject which those attending the conference should be considering when they met. The minister then analysed the resolution in a sort of academic way. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that all these resolutions should be construed in a broad way. They lay down a general principle. For example, in this case, the principle is that it is a desirable thing, in the opinion of this house, that assistance should be given by the federal government to such a worthy object as education. He stated that the provinces and the municipalities had not been mentioned specifically in the resolution. It seems to me it should not be necessary to do that.
Education
Undoubtedly it was intended toy the mover of the resolution that the aid go to the provinces as the repository of the responsibility for education.
